notes:
=== DLL Injection and Hijacking ===
Force a process to load attacker-controlled code — inheriting the process's privileges.

=== DLL INJECTION TECHNIQUES ===
LoadLibrary injection (classic, well-monitored by AV/EDR):
  1. OpenProcess → target process handle
  2. VirtualAllocEx → allocate memory in target for DLL path
  3. WriteProcessMemory → write DLL path into allocated memory
  4. GetProcAddress(LoadLibraryA) → same address in all processes (kernel32 ASLR exception)
  5. CreateRemoteThread → start thread in target at LoadLibraryA with DLL path as arg
  Drawback: CreateRemoteThread + LoadLibrary are heavily monitored by EDR

Manual mapping (avoids LoadLibrary API hook):
  Read DLL as raw bytes → map PE sections into target manually → resolve imports → execute DllMain
  Harder to detect but complex to implement

Reflective DLL injection (no LoadLibrary, no Windows loader):
  DLL contains its own ReflectiveLoader export
  Self-loads from arbitrary memory location, resolves its own imports
  No trace in standard module list — hardest to detect

=== DLL HIJACKING (most practical for privilege escalation) ===
Exploits Windows DLL search order:
  1. Application directory
  2. System directory (System32)
  3. Windows directory
  4. Current directory
  5. Directories in PATH

Identifying hijack opportunities:
  Process Monitor (Procmon) → filter on "Load Image" + "NAME NOT FOUND"
  Shows DLLs the process tries to load but cannot find → prime hijack targets

INVALID LIBRARY HIJACK (missing DLL):
  Process looks for DLL that doesn't exist → place file with that name in searched directory
  DllMain DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH case executes automatically when DLL loads
  No interaction needed after placement

PROXY DLL HIJACK (DLL exists, must keep working):
  Rename original: library.dll → library.o.dll
  Create malicious proxy with same exports that calls original functions
  Application sees no errors, proxy code also executes

=== PRIVILEGE ESCALATION APPLICATION ===
Target: SYSTEM-level process or auto-elevating binary that loads a DLL from user-writable directory
Example: UAC bypass via srrstr.dll (see uac-bypass-srrstr card) uses this exact technique
Procmon on elevated process → find NAME NOT FOUND in writable PATH locations → place malicious DLL

=== CHAINING CONTEXT ===
Auto-elevating binary + writable PATH directory → DLL hijack → UAC bypass → full token
SYSTEM process loading DLL from writable directory → DLL hijack → SYSTEM code execution
Service startup DLL loading from writable path → hijack → SYSTEM at next service start
Persistence: DLL hijack persists across reboots/service restarts

=== WHAT TO LOOK FOR ===
Run Procmon on target processes to find missing DLL loads
Services loading DLLs from C:\ProgramData or user profile directories
Applications with custom DLL paths in insecure locations
auto-elevate manifest in binary (check with sigcheck.exe or strings on binary manifest) OSCP Ch16 pattern: (1) confirm app tries to load a missing DLL (ProcMon filter: Process Name=app.exe, Operation=CreateFile, Result=NAME NOT FOUND, Path contains DLL name); (2) confirm write access to app directory; (3) x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc malicious.cpp --shared -o missing.dll; (4) deploy to app dir (first in search order); (5) wait for privileged user to launch app. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 16 (Windows Privilege Escalation).

name: DLL Hijacking - Missing / Proxy DLL
command: # place a malicious DLL earlier in the search order than the real one
description: If an application loads a DLL by name from a writable/earlier search-order location, drop a malicious DLL there. Proxy-DLL technique: rename the real lib to library.o.dll and supply a tamper DLL named library.dll that forwards exports while running your code in DllMain.

defense.why_it_works: When an application loads a DLL without specifying an absolute path, Windows resolves it via DLL search order: application directory, System32, Windows directory, then directories in PATH. If the application directory (or another path before System32) is writable by the attacker, planting a malicious DLL with the expected name causes it to be loaded instead of the legitimate one, executing attacker code in the application's security context.
defense.prerequisites: A target application that loads a DLL without full path (identified via Process Monitor or known vulnerability). Write access to the application directory or a directory in PATH before System32. Application must be executed (by the target user or a scheduled mechanism).
defense.impact: Code execution in the context of the application loading the DLL. If the application runs as SYSTEM, admin, or another privileged account, this achieves privilege escalation.
defense.detection: Process Monitor: 'NAME NOT FOUND' for DLL load attempts in writable directories. New DLL files in application directories. Sysmon Event 7: DLL loaded from unexpected path. File creation monitoring on application directories.
defense.artifacts: Process Monitor: DLL load failure then success from unexpected path | Sysmon Event 7: image load from non-System32 path | File: new DLL in application directory | Process: elevated execution following DLL plant
defense.prevention: Use absolute paths when loading DLLs (LoadLibrary with full path). Restrict write access on application directories to SYSTEM and Administrators. Enable SafeDllSearchMode (default enabled). Apply code signing — load only signed DLLs in controlled applications.
defense.misconfiguration: Application directory has write access for standard users. Application loads DLL by name only without full path. SafeDllSearchMode disabled. No file integrity monitoring on application directories.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Process Monitor shows:
# DISM.exe -> CreateFile -> C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Temp\version.dll -> NAME NOT FOUND
# Plant malicious DLL:
copy C:\Tools\shell.dll C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Temp\version.dll
# Run DISM or trigger application -> DLL hijacked
defense.secure_config:
# Fix application (developer-side):
# Use SetDllDirectory('') + LoadLibrary('C:\Program Files\App\lib.dll')

# OS-side: restrict app directory permissions:
icacls 'C:\Program Files\VulnApp' /inheritance:r /grant 'SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F' /grant 'Administrators:(OI)(CI)F'

# Enable SafeDllSearchMode:
reg add HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session\ Manager /v SafeDllSearchMode /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
